note: One entry per clip. 'segments' is the narration: one line per on-screen caption, in the order the captions appear in the scene.

segments.caption: A model cannot know your hospital's own protocols.
segments.text: A language model learns from public text, so it cannot know your hospital's own protocols. Asked when antibiotics must start under our sepsis protocol, it says three hours: a reasonable national figure, but not our rule.

segments.caption: Split the documents into chunks and embed each chunk once.
segments.text: Retrieval starts by splitting the hospital's documents into chunks. Almanac used chunks of one thousand tokens. Each chunk is embedded once into a vector, which in Almanac had one thousand five hundred thirty-six numbers.

segments.caption: Embed the question and score every chunk by cosine similarity.
segments.text: At question time, the question is embedded the same way and compared with every chunk by co-sine similarity. Here the three best chunks score zero point eight six, zero point seven nine, and zero point six two.

segments.caption: Only chunks above a threshold pass: Almanac used λ = 0.83.
segments.text: Only chunks that score above a threshold are passed on. Almanac used a threshold, lambda, of zero point eight three, so here only the first chunk, from the sepsis protocol, passes.

segments.caption: If nothing passes, the published Almanac falls back on the model's own knowledge.
segments.text: A second question, about rattlesnake bites, finds no good match: its best score is only zero point seven one. The published Almanac then falls back on the model's own knowledge. The preprint version abstained instead, and said the answer was not found in the sources.

segments.caption: The passing chunk goes into the prompt with its source, and the answer cites it.
segments.text: The passing chunk is pasted into the prompt, together with its source. The model now answers within one hour, which is what the synthetic protocol says, and it cites section two of that protocol.

segments.caption: Almanac ranked first of four systems on 314 clinical questions.
segments.text: Clinicians compared Almanac with Chat G P T four, Bing, and Bard on three hundred fourteen clinical questions. Almanac ranked first for factuality, completeness, and preference, and its citations were correct ninety-one percent of the time.

segments.caption: Read with care: the adversarial wins come mostly from declining to answer.
segments.text: Read these results with care. Against adversarial prompts, Almanac scored one hundred percent and Chat G P T four seven percent, mostly because Almanac declined to answer. The questions and the grading came from the study's own clinicians, and only twenty-five questions are public.

segments.caption: An agent repeats a cycle: thought, action, observation.
segments.text: An agent works in a loop of thought, action, and observation. Our task, for the synthetic patient P zero zero one: is the potassium rising, and is it abnormal?

segments.caption: Thought, then action: the model writes the tool call as JSON.
segments.text: First the model writes a thought: I need the last three potassium results. Then it writes an action, a tool call in JSON, naming the tool, get labs, and its arguments: the patient, the test, and how many results.

segments.caption: Observation: the program runs the tool and adds the result to the context.
segments.text: The program, not the model, runs the tool against the record and appends the result to the context: four point six, five point one, and five point six millimoles per liter.

segments.caption: Thought: rising, and 5.6 is above the usual upper limit of about 5.0.
segments.text: The model reads the observation and writes a new thought: the potassium is rising, and five point six is above the usual upper limit of about five point zero. Its last action is finish, with the answer and the values.

segments.caption: A tool call is just text in an agreed format; ReAct learned it from a few examples.
segments.text: A tool call is just text that the model writes in an agreed format. ReAct got this behavior from a few worked examples in the prompt, with no training at all. Today's models are post-trained to write tool calls, as in week five.

segments.caption: ALFWorld: ReAct succeeded 71% of the time, versus 45% for acting without thoughts.
segments.text: On ALFWorld, a text-based benchmark of household tasks, the best of six ReAct prompts succeeded seventy-one percent of the time, versus forty-five for acting without thoughts. Even the worst ReAct prompt beat the best acting-only one.

segments.caption: HotpotQA: ReAct alone trailed chain of thought; combining the two did best.
segments.text: On HotpotQA, multi-hop questions answered from Wikipedia, ReAct alone scored twenty-seven point four, below chain of thought at twenty-nine point four. Falling back to chain of thought with self-consistency when ReAct got stuck did best, at thirty-five point one.

segments.caption: Grounding removed hallucinations, but ReAct failed through reasoning errors instead.
segments.text: The authors labelled fifty failed runs of each method by hand. Hallucination caused fifty-six percent of chain-of-thought failures and none of ReAct's. But forty-seven percent of ReAct's failures were reasoning errors, such as repeating the same step.

segments.caption: Every step of an agent can fail.
segments.text: Every step of an agent is a chance to fail. It can pick the wrong tool, pass the wrong patient number, misread a result, or repeat the same call again and again. In ReAct, most failures were reasoning errors like these.

segments.caption: If each step succeeds with probability 0.95, n steps succeed with 0.95ⁿ.
segments.text: Suppose each step succeeds ninety-five percent of the time, and steps fail independently. Then a task of n steps succeeds with zero point nine five to the power n: zero point seven seven for five steps, zero point six for ten, and only zero point three six for twenty.

segments.caption: At 0.99 per step: 0.90 for 10 steps and 0.82 for 20.
segments.text: Raise each step to ninety-nine percent, and ten steps succeed ninety percent of the time, twenty steps eighty-two percent. A small gain per step makes a large difference for long tasks.

segments.caption: Check results, and give the agent read-only tools.
segments.text: Mitigations start with the tools. The agent checks its own results, for example by re-reading the lab table, and a mismatch stops the task. It gets only read-only tools, such as get labs and get meds, never one that places orders or sends messages.

segments.caption: Any action that changes care waits for a clinician's approval.
segments.text: Any action that changes care, such as an order or a message to a patient, stops at a checkpoint. The agent proposes it, here a repeat potassium and an ECG, and a clinician approves or rejects it before anything happens.

segments.caption: Retrieval grounds answers, tools let the model act, and every step can fail.
segments.text: To sum up: retrieval grounds answers in sources, tools let the model act on real data through text it writes, and every added step is another chance to fail. So check results, limit the tools, and ask a clinician.
